# Slack vs Element (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Element are two popular communication platforms designed for teams and organizations. This comparison is beneficial for those looking to switch from a proprietary platform to a self-hosted, open-source solution, with the core use case being team collaboration and communication. The key reason someone would switch is to gain control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Element is free and self-hosted, while Slack has a per-user monthly fee.
* Data ownership: Element allows teams to have full control over their data, while Slack stores data on its servers.
* Setup complexity: Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, while Slack is easier to get started with.
* Scalability: Element can be more scalable than Slack, as it can be self-hosted on the team's own servers.
* Integration difference: Element has a more limited set of integrations compared to Slack, but it supports Matrix protocol for interoperability.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Element |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1450-$3000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
### Slack
* Easy to use and set up
* Large community and wide adoption
* Wide range of integrations available
* Good mobile app support
* Limited control over data and security
### Element
* Self-hosted and open-source
* Full control over data and security
* Scalable and customizable
* Supports Matrix protocol for interoperability
* Limited integrations and mobile app support

## When to Choose Each
Slack is a good choice for small to medium-sized teams who prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations. It's also a good option for teams who don't require full control over their data and security. Element, on the other hand, is a good choice for larger teams or organizations who require full control over their data and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool.
2. Set up an Element server and configure it to your needs.
3. Import your Slack data into Element using the Element import tool.
4. Configure any necessary integrations and settings in Element.
5. Test and verify that everything is working as expected.

## Our Take
Element is not yet production-ready for most users, as it still lacks some of the features and polish of Slack. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Element's mobile app support is still limited, and may not be as seamless as Slack's. However, for teams who require full control over their data and security, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution, Element is a good choice.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams who don't require a wide range of integrations and want to save on costs
* Medium-sized teams who require full control over their data and security
* Large teams who are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining a self-hosted solution
* Teams who don't need mobile app support
* Teams who are already using Matrix protocol and want to take advantage of interoperability

## FAQ
### Can I use Element for free?
Yes, Element is free and open-source, and can be self-hosted on your own servers.
### Is Element as easy to use as Slack?
No, Element requires more technical expertise to set up and maintain, but it offers more control over data and security.
### Can I integrate Element with other tools?
Yes, Element supports Matrix protocol for interoperability, and has a growing list of integrations available.
### Is Element suitable for large teams?
Yes, Element is scalable and can be self-hosted on your own servers, making it a good option for large teams.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Element?
Yes, you can export your Slack data and import it into Element using the Element import tool.

# Slack vs Mattermost (2026)

## Overview
Slack and Mattermost are both team communication platforms designed to facilitate collaboration and productivity among team members. This comparison is beneficial for teams considering switching from Slack to Mattermost, particularly those prioritizing data ownership and cost-effectiveness. The core use case for both tools is to provide a centralized platform for team communication, and the key reason someone would switch is to gain more control over their data and reduce costs.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Mattermost offers a free, self-hosted option, while Slack charges per user.
* Data ownership: Mattermost allows teams to self-host and maintain full control over their data, whereas Slack stores data on its proprietary servers.
* Setup complexity: Slack has a more straightforward setup process, while Mattermost requires more technical expertise for self-hosting.
* Scalability: Mattermost is designed to scale horizontally, making it more suitable for large teams, while Slack's scalability is limited by its proprietary architecture.
* Integration with GitHub: Mattermost has native integration with GitHub, allowing for seamless workflow management, whereas Slack requires a third-party integration.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Slack | Mattermost |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $7.25-$15/user/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT / AGPL |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $362.50-$750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $1,450-$3,000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Slack:**
* Easy to set up and use
* Wide range of integrations with third-party apps
* Robust mobile apps
* Good customer support
* Limited control over data ownership
**Mattermost:**
* Self-hosted option for full data control
* Highly customizable and extensible
* Scalable architecture
* Native integration with GitHub
* Steeper learning curve due to self-hosting requirements

## When to Choose Each
Slack is suitable for small to medium-sized teams that prioritize ease of use and a wide range of integrations with third-party apps. It's ideal for teams that don't require full control over their data and are willing to pay a premium for a hassle-free experience. On the other hand, Mattermost is designed for larger teams or organizations that require high levels of customization, scalability, and data control. It's perfect for teams with technical expertise and a need for self-hosting, such as open-source projects or enterprises with strict data security requirements.

Mattermost is also a good choice for teams that are already invested in the GitHub ecosystem and want to streamline their workflow management. In contrast, Slack is a better fit for teams that rely heavily on third-party integrations and don't require the level of customization that Mattermost offers.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Slack data using the Slack API or a third-party tool like Slack Exporter.
2. Set up a Mattermost instance on your own server or use a cloud hosting provider.
3. Use the Mattermost import tool to migrate your Slack data, including channels, users, and messages.
4. Configure your Mattermost instance to match your team's requirements, including customizing the interface and setting up integrations.
5. Test your Mattermost instance to ensure a smooth transition for your team.

## Our Take
Mattermost is a production-ready alternative to Slack for teams that require high levels of customization and data control. However, it may not be the best choice for small teams or those without technical expertise, as it requires self-hosting and has a steeper learning curve. One specific technical limitation worth knowing is that Mattermost's mobile apps are not as polished as Slack's, which may be a concern for teams with a high number of mobile users. We recommend Mattermost for teams that value data ownership and customization, but suggest that small teams or those without technical expertise stick with Slack.

## Who Should Switch
* Large teams (100+ users) that require high levels of customization and data control
* Open-source projects that need a self-hosted solution for collaboration
* Enterprises with strict data security requirements
* Teams already invested in the GitHub ecosystem
* Small teams (less than 20 users) that don't require many integrations and want to save on costs

## FAQ
### Can I self-host Mattermost on my own server?
Yes, Mattermost offers a self-hosted option, allowing teams to maintain full control over their data and infrastructure.
### Is Mattermost free?
Mattermost is free to use, but self-hosting requires server costs and technical expertise.
### Can I migrate my Slack data to Mattermost?
Yes, Mattermost offers an import tool to migrate Slack data, including channels, users, and messages.
### Does Mattermost have mobile apps?
Yes, Mattermost has mobile apps for Android and iOS, but they may not be as polished as Slack's.
### Is Mattermost suitable for small teams?
Mattermost can be suitable for small teams, but it may require more technical expertise and have a steeper learning curve than Slack.

title: Discord vs Element
comparison_markdown:
# Discord vs Element

## Overview

Chat platform popular with gaming and developer communities. is a popular proprietary tool in the communication space. Element is a free, open-source alternative that gives organizations complete control over their data and deployment.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: Discord costs Free / $9.99/month; Element is Free (self-hosted)
- **License**: Discord is Proprietary; Element is Apache 2.0
- **Data ownership**: Element can be self-hosted so your data stays on infrastructure you control
- **Vendor lock-in**: Element eliminates dependency on a single commercial vendor
- **Community**: Element has an active open-source community contributing features and fixes

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | Discord | Element |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $9.99/month | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | Apache 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### Discord

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### Element

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [element-hq/element-web](https://github.com/element-hq/element-web) * ~11k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose Discord if:** Discord is the right choice when you need the most polished user experience, the broadest integration ecosystem, and professional support with SLA guarantees.

**Choose Element if:** Element is ideal for privacy-conscious teams, organizations with strict data sovereignty requirements, or anyone wanting to eliminate per-seat subscription costs.

## Migration Path

Export your data from Discord in its standard export format, review Element import documentation, and plan a pilot period where both tools run in parallel.

## Our Take

Element is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid Discord tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your Element instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for Discord, switching to self-hosted Element will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on Discord until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated Discord paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is Element free to use?
Yes. Element is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from Discord to Element?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your Discord data, follow the Element import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does Element get regular updates?
Yes. Element has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use Element without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if Element development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [Discord](https://discord.com) and [Element](https://element.io) before making decisions.*
meta_description: Element is a free, self-hosted alternative to Discord. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: GitHub vs GitLab
comparison_markdown:
# GitHub vs GitLab

## Overview

GitHub is the world largest code hosting platform, owned by Microsoft, with 100 million developers. GitLab is a complete DevOps platform that can be fully self-hosted, offering everything from Git hosting to CI/CD and container registries.

## Key Differences

- **Cost**: GitHub free tier is generous; GitLab Community Edition is fully free to self-host
- **CI/CD**: GitLab has more powerful built-in CI/CD pipelines; GitHub Actions is catching up
- **Self-hosting**: GitLab is designed to be self-hosted; GitHub Enterprise self-hosted is expensive
- **Feature scope**: GitLab is a complete DevSecOps platform; GitHub focuses on developer collaboration
- **Community**: GitHub has a dramatically larger open-source community and project discoverability

## Pricing Comparison

| Aspect | GitHub | GitLab |
|--------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Base pricing | Free / $7-$21/user | Free (self-hosted) |
| License | Proprietary | MIT (CE) |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Cost at 50 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Cost at 200 users | See pricing page | $0/month (self-hosted) |
| Vendor lock-in | High | None |

## Pros and Cons

### GitHub

**Pros:**
- Polished, professionally designed user interface
- Large ecosystem of official integrations
- Managed infrastructure with no server maintenance required
- Enterprise SLA and dedicated support available
- Mobile apps are well-maintained and reliable

**Cons:**
- Significant per-user monthly cost that scales linearly with team size
- Your data is stored on the vendor infrastructure
- No ability to inspect or modify the source code
- Feature roadmap controlled entirely by the vendor
- Risk of pricing changes, acquisition, or discontinuation

### GitLab

**Pros:**
- Free to self-host with costs only for server infrastructure
- Complete data ownership and privacy control
- Source code is auditable and modifiable
- Active open-source community
- No vendor lock-in or risk of sudden pricing changes
> GitHub: [gitlabhq/gitlabhq](https://github.com/gitlabhq/gitlabhq) * ~24k stars

**Cons:**
- Requires technical knowledge to self-host and maintain
- May lack some advanced features found in the proprietary version
- Support relies on community forums rather than a paid helpdesk
- UI polish may lag behind the proprietary tool
- You are responsible for updates, backups, and security patches

## When to Choose Each

**Choose GitHub if:** GitHub suits open-source projects wanting maximum community visibility or teams deeply integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

**Choose GitLab if:** GitLab self-hosted is ideal for enterprises needing full control over their DevOps stack or regulated industries.

## Migration Path

GitLab provides a GitHub importer that migrates repositories, issues, PRs, wikis, and milestones. Update CI configuration from GitHub Actions to GitLab CI/CD YAML format.

## Our Take

GitLab is production-ready for most teams willing to invest a few hours in setup. The self-hosted version gives you identical or better functionality to the paid GitHub tiers, with no recurring per-seat cost.

The main technical limitation worth knowing: you are responsible for your own backups, updates, and uptime. If your server goes down, so does your GitLab instance. Plan for this with automated backups and a monitoring alert.

Our recommendation: if your team has at least one developer and you are paying more than $100/month for GitHub, switching to self-hosted GitLab will pay for itself within the first month. If nobody on your team is comfortable with Linux or Docker, stay on GitHub until you have that resource.

## Who Should Switch

- Startups under 20 people paying per-seat fees they cannot yet justify
- Dev teams who already self-host other tools and have the ops knowledge
- Organizations in jurisdictions with strict data residency requirements
- Teams who have evaluated GitHub paid features and only use the basics
- Founders and solopreneurs who want the functionality without the subscription

## FAQ

### Is GitLab free to use?
Yes. GitLab is free to self-host. Your only cost is the server, typically $6-$12/month on a VPS provider like DigitalOcean or Vultr.

### How hard is it to migrate from GitHub to GitLab?
For most teams, migration takes 2-4 hours. Export your GitHub data, follow the GitLab import guide, and test with a small group before switching everyone over.

### Does GitLab get regular updates?
Yes. GitLab has an active open-source community with regular releases. Check the GitHub repository for release frequency.

### Can I use GitLab without technical knowledge?
You need basic comfort with a VPS and command line. If that feels unfamiliar, there are managed hosting options that handle the server for you at a modest cost.

### What happens if GitLab development stops?
Because the source code is open, you can continue running whatever version you have indefinitely. You can also fork the project or switch to another tool at your own pace — no vendor can shut off your instance.

---
*Data sourced July 2026. Pricing and features change. Verify at [GitHub](https://github.com) and [GitLab](https://gitlab.com) before making decisions.*
meta_description: GitLab is a free, self-hosted alternative to GitHub. Compare pricing, features, and migration steps. See full comparison.

title: Figma vs Penpot
comparison_markdown:
# Figma vs Penpot (2026)

## Overview
Figma and Penpot are both design and prototyping tools used for user interface (UI) and user experience (UX) design. This comparison benefits designers, product managers, and developers who are looking for a tool to create, test, and refine their digital products. The key reason someone would switch from Figma to Penpot is to take advantage of Penpot's free and self-hosted options, which can be more cost-effective for large teams or organizations with specific data ownership requirements.

## Key Differences
* Cost: Figma offers a free plan with limited features, while Penpot is completely free and open-source.
* Data Ownership: Figma stores design files on its servers, while Penpot allows users to self-host and have full control over their data.
* Setup Complexity: Figma has a more straightforward setup process, while Penpot requires more technical expertise to set up and self-host.
* Scalability: Figma is designed to handle large teams and complex projects, while Penpot's scalability is still being developed and tested.
* Integration with Other Tools: Figma has a more extensive library of plugins and integrations with other design and development tools, while Penpot's integration options are still limited.

## Pricing Comparison
| Aspect | Figma | Penpot |
|--------|----------|---------|
| Base Cost | $12-$75/user/month | Free |
| License | Proprietary | MPL 2.0 |
| Self-hosting | Not available | Available |
| Per-user cost at 50 users | $600-$3750/month | $0 (server cost only) |
| Per-user cost at 200 users | $2400-$15000/month | $0 (server cost only) |

## Pros and Cons
**Figma:**
* Pros:
	+ User-friendly interface and collaborative features
	+ Large community and extensive library of plugins and integrations
	+ Scalable and reliable infrastructure
	+ Regular updates with new features and improvements
* Cons:
	+ Expensive for large teams or enterprises
	+ Limited control over data ownership and storage
	+ Dependence on Figma's servers and infrastructure
**Penpot:**
* Pros:
	+ Free and open-source, with self-hosting options
	+ Full control over data ownership and storage
	+ Customizable and extensible through plugins and integrations
	+ Community-driven development and support
* Cons:
	+ Steeper learning curve and more technical expertise required
	+ Limited scalability and reliability compared to Figma
	+ Still in active development, with some features and integrations missing

## When to Choose Each
Figma is the better choice for large teams, enterprises, or organizations that require a reliable and scalable design and prototyping tool, with a wide range of integrations and plugins. It is also suitable for teams that prioritize ease of use and a user-friendly interface. On the other hand, Penpot is ideal for smaller teams, startups, or individuals who value data ownership and control, and are comfortable with self-hosting and customizing their design tool. It is also a good option for teams with limited budgets or those who want to avoid vendor lock-in.

Penpot is the better choice for teams that require a high degree of customization and extensibility, and are willing to invest time and resources into setting up and maintaining their own design tool. It is also suitable for teams that prioritize community-driven development and support, and want to contribute to the growth and improvement of the tool.

## Migration Path
1. Export your Figma design files in the Sketch format (.sketch) or JSON format.
2. Set up a Penpot server and create a new project.
3. Use the Penpot import tool to import your design files into the new project.
4. Review and update your design files to ensure compatibility with Penpot's features and plugins.
5. Collaborate with your team to test and refine your designs in Penpot.

## Our Take
Penpot is still in active development, and while it shows great promise, it may not be production-ready for most users right now. The tool is constantly evolving, with new features and improvements being added regularly. However, one specific technical limitation worth knowing before switching is that Penpot's scalability and reliability are still being developed and tested, which may impact large teams or enterprises.

Penpot's self-hosting options and data ownership features make it an attractive choice for teams that value control and customization. However, Figma's user-friendly interface, extensive library of plugins and integrations, and reliable infrastructure make it a more suitable choice for teams that prioritize ease of use and scalability. Our clear and direct recommendation is that teams who value data ownership and control, and are comfortable with self-hosting and customizing their design tool, should consider switching to Penpot. On the other hand, teams that prioritize ease of use, scalability, and reliability should stick with Figma.

## Who Should Switch
* Small teams (less than 10 users) who value data ownership and control
* Startups or individuals with limited budgets who want to avoid vendor lock-in
* Teams that require custom plugins or integrations not available in Figma
* Organizations with specific data storage or security requirements
* Designers or teams who want to contribute to the growth and improvement of an open-source design tool

## FAQ
### Can I use Penpot for free?
Yes, Penpot is completely free and open-source, with self-hosting options available.
### Is Penpot compatible with Figma design files?
Yes, Penpot can import Figma design files in the Sketch format (.sketch) or JSON format.
### Does Penpot have the same features as Figma?
No, Penpot is still in active development, and some features and integrations are still missing or in development.
### Can I self-host Penpot on my own server?
Yes, Penpot provides self-hosting options, which allow you to have full control over your data and infrastructure.
### Is Penpot suitable for large teams or enterprises?
Not yet, Penpot's scalability and reliability are still being developed and tested, which may impact large teams or enterprises.
